---
title: "Methods: sorting motifs by subject"
description: "How the Sjónabók gallery groups patterns by what they depict (birds, flowers, deer and more): a practical guide to using AI to sort a collection, with a person making every decision."
---

Many Sjónabók patterns depict something: a bird, a flower in a vase, a reindeer, a heart. This page explains how we group them by subject, step by step, so that anyone can
check the result or repeat the method on their own collection. Every script, setting and label is
in the [Sjonabok repository](https://github.com/HiDefTextiles/Sjonabok/tree/main/analysis/subjects).

::: {.heimild}
**The rule we follow: the computer proposes, a person decides.** No subject shown in the gallery
was set by a computer. AI is used to put similar charts next to each other so that a person can
label them quickly and consistently. Every label carries the name of the person who set it and
the date.
:::

## Why not let the AI decide?

Image models are trained mostly on photographs. A Sjónabók chart is different: a bird may be
10 × 10 cells of black and white, drawn in a style several centuries old. A model can tell that
two charts *look alike*, and that is useful, but it cannot be trusted to say that a chart *is a
bird*. A wrong label in a public gallery is worse than no label. So the AI does the tedious part,
sorting 600 charts into small piles of look-alikes, and a person does the part that needs
knowledge.

## The workflow at a glance

| Step | Done by | What happens | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Units | Computer | Pick what to compare: a whole motif, or one repeat of a band | `units.csv` |
| 2. Shape distance | Computer | Compare every pair of charts cell by cell, ignoring flips, turns and shifts | `shape_dist.csv` |
| 3. Image model | Computer | Describe each chart with a pretrained image model and compare the descriptions | `embed_dist.csv` |
| 4. Clusters | Computer | Put the charts into about 50 small piles of look-alikes | `clusters.csv` |
| 5. Review | Person | Look at each pile, name its subject, pick out the odd ones | `review.csv` → `subjects.csv` |
| 6. Suggestions | Computer | For charts not yet reviewed, suggest the subject of their nearest labelled neighbours | `suggestions.csv` |
| 7. Gallery | Computer | Show reviewed subjects and main groups as filters | the *Main group* and *Subject* filters |
| Check | Person | Label 40 random charts one at a time, settle the differences | `fairtest.csv` |

Steps 1 to 4 and 6 can be rerun at any time and give the same result. Step 5 is the only one
whose output is written by a person, and a rerun never changes it.

## Step 1: what is compared {#units}

A stand-alone motif or rosette is compared as the whole chart, with its empty margin trimmed.
A border band repeats one figure many times, so it is compared on one repeat (the
[repeat unit](about.qmd#repeats)), otherwise a band of six birds would look nothing like a single
bird. The first round, the *pilot*, covers the 233 motifs and rosettes. Bands follow once the
pilot has been reviewed.

## Step 2: shape distance {#shape}

Each chart is shrunk to a 16 × 16 grey picture and compared with every other chart in all eight
turned and mirrored positions. The best match counts (a correlation between the pictures), and
the distance is one minus that match. This is the same comparison as
[similar patterns](about.qmd#similar). It is exact and easy to explain, and it is good at finding
copies and close variants of the same figure. It is poor at meaning: a bird with raised wings and
one with lowered wings can be far apart.

## Step 3: a pretrained image model {#embedding}

An *image model* is a neural network that has already learnt, from millions of pictures, to
describe an image as a list of numbers (an *embedding*). Pictures that look alike to people get
similar lists. We use [DINOv2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07193), an openly published model, in
its smallest size (ViT-S/14, loaded with the `timm` library from Hugging Face), which describes each picture with 384 numbers and runs on an
ordinary laptop without a graphics card. We do not train or change the model.

For each chart we:

1. draw it black on white in a 224 × 224 square, enlarging whole cells so the edges stay sharp;
2. do this in all eight turned and mirrored positions and average the eight descriptions, so a
   bird facing left and one facing right are described the same way;
3. compare two charts by the angle between their descriptions (one minus the cosine similarity).

The model sees the overall form, a beak and legs, a stem with leaves, better than the cell-by-cell
comparison does. It can also be fooled by texture or by how dense a chart is, which is why its
result is only a proposal.

## Step 4: clusters {#clusters}

The charts are grouped by the image-model distance from step 3. We also tried averaging it with
the shape distance from step 2 (each first turned into ranks between 0 and 1 so they share a
scale). On the pilot that mixed deer, stars and flowers in the same piles, while the image model
alone kept the animals together, so the shape distance now gets weight 0. It is kept in the
code, because it is used when the image model cannot be run and it may help other collections.
The charts are then grouped with
[hierarchical clustering](https://search.r-project.org/R/refmans/stats/html/hclust.html)
in R (Ward's method). This builds a family tree of the charts, joining the most alike first,
and the tree is cut into 50 piles.

Fifty is deliberately more than the number of subjects. Small, pure piles are quick to review;
large piles mix subjects and have to be sorted chart by chart. Two piles of birds are no problem,
they get the same label. The piles are numbered along the tree, so neighbouring numbers look alike.

We also built a third distance from what the gallery already measures about each chart:
its symmetry scores and symmetry group, its form (share of filled cells, width to height, number of
separate pieces) and its provenance (the same manuscript, and the same page, count as closer).
After the first review we checked how well each distance predicts the subjects the reviewer gave,
by asking which subject a chart's five nearest charts have. The image model came out ahead, but
that check is unfair to the other distances, and we no longer quote its numbers (an outside
review could not reproduce them from the labels as committed).

It is unfair because the reviewer labelled piles that the image model had made. So we ran a fair test (`make sample`): 40 charts drawn at random with a fixed seed and
labelled one at a time, outside any pile. Two charts were labelled *not sure*, which leaves 38.

The first surprise was the reviewer. The same person had given 20 of the 40 charts a different set
of subjects in the piles than on their own, almost always star, cross or geometric (a few only
gained or lost a second subject). Those 20 were
looked at again on a *settle* page that showed both earlier answers, and the new answer replaced
both. Then each distance was scored again, guessing a chart's subject from its five nearest
labelled charts:

| Distance | 12 subjects | 3 main groups |
|---|---|---|
| Image model | 50% | 66–74% |
| Cell-by-cell shape | 50–53% | 68–71% |
| Gallery measures (symmetry, form, provenance) | 37–42% | 68% |
| Image model and gallery measures, 2 : 1 | 39–55% | 68–79% |
| Always guess the most common (star; ornament) | 24% | 53% |

Each range runs over two pools of neighbours: all charts labelled in the piles, and only the other
38 fair-test charts. With 38 charts the uncertainty is large (a 95% interval of about ±13
percentage points), so a difference of three charts is within chance and no distance is clearly
best. Settling can also have nudged a few labels towards the piles: of the 20, 13 kept the answer
given on its own, 3 the pile answer, and 4 got a new one. The image model stays the default and the gallery measures keep weight 0
(`W_META` in the Makefile). The clearer lesson is in the second column: at the level of the
[main groups](#groups) the computer is right about three times in four, and before settling the
reviewer's two answers shared a main group for 34 of the 38 charts (identical main groups for 29).

We first tried *average linkage*. It joined most charts into one pile of 55 and left many piles
of one, so we changed to Ward's method, which keeps piles of similar size (largest 18 in the pilot).

## Step 5: the review {#review}

The reviewer opens a review page that works on a phone: one card per pile, with every chart drawn
from its 0/1 file. For each pile they tap:

- **subject**: one word from the [subject list](https://github.com/HiDefTextiles/Sjonabok/blob/main/analysis/subjects/vocabulary.csv)
  (bird, flower, tree, deer, other animal, heart, star, cross, letters, geometric, not sure). A chart can have several subjects, for example a bird on a flowering branch.
- **exceptions**: tap a chart that does not fit to see it large and give it its own subject.
- **mixed**: if the pile is too varied, it is left for a finer cut in the next round.

The answers are exported as `review.csv`, one row per pile. The page is in the repository
(`analysis/subjects/review/`, started with `make review`), so the next round, or another collection,
can be reviewed the same way. In our pilot one person reviewed 34 piles in about eight minutes.

`make labels` then writes one row per chart into `subjects.csv`: the chart, its subjects, the
reviewer's name, the date and any note. This file is the result of the whole method, and it is the
only file a person writes.

## Step 6: suggestions for the rest {#suggestions}

Once some charts are labelled, each unlabelled chart gets a suggestion: the most common subject
among its five nearest labelled charts, with how many of the five agree. Suggestions go into the
next review round to speed it up. They are never shown in the gallery as a subject.

## Step 7: the gallery {#gallery}

When the gallery is built, `subjects.csv` is read and each pattern gets its reviewed subjects.
They appear as the *Main group* and *Subject* filters and in the pattern view. Charts not yet reviewed are listed
as *Not yet sorted*.

## Main groups {#groups}

Star, cross and geometric are where people disagree, the same person included. So each subject
also belongs to one of four main groups ([`groups.csv`](https://github.com/HiDefTextiles/Sjonabok/blob/main/analysis/subjects/groups.csv)):

| Main group | Subjects |
|---|---|
| Animals | bird, deer or reindeer, other animal |
| Plants | flower, tree |
| Ornament | star or rose, cross, heart, geometric |
| Letters | letters, monograms, words |

The gallery offers *Main group* as its first subject filter, because it is the safer one. A chart
with subjects in two groups, for example a rose with a flower at its centre, is in both, like the
overlap of two circles in a Venn diagram. In the pilot 3 of 231 charts sit in such an overlap
(Ornament and Plants); more will follow as charts are labelled with several subjects.

## Features such as knots {#features}

Some things are not a subject but a feature that any chart can have: knotwork, small flowers inside
a larger motif, a frame. These are kept in a separate list
([`features.csv`](https://github.com/HiDefTextiles/Sjonabok/blob/main/analysis/subjects/features.csv)),
so that a rosette can be *Ornament* and have *knotwork*, and a solo flower (subject *Flower*) is
kept apart from a motif with small flowers in it (feature *Small flowers*).

For knots the computer helps with a measure taken straight from the 0/1 chart (`make knots`):
interlace leaves many small enclosed openings between its strands, and its strands run diagonally,
so cells touch only at their corners. Every chart is ranked by these two measures, and the reviewer
marks the most knot-like ones *Knot* or *No knot* on a phone page. As always, the ranking only
decides the order; the reviewer decides what is a knot.

## What the computer misses, in the reviewer's words {#clues}

After the weights were learnt, the computer still put 44 labelled charts in the wrong main group.
The reviewer went through 41 of them on a phone page and tapped what told her the group
([`misses_clues.csv`](https://github.com/HiDefTextiles/Sjonabok/blob/main/analysis/subjects/misses_clues.csv)):
for animals *wings or tail* (11) and *head and legs* (4); for plants *petals* (7) and *stem or
leaves* (4); for ornament *outline shape* (7) and *needs repeat* (4). Four labels were wrong and
were corrected, and letters became a main group of their own.

Each clue became a measure taken straight from the 0/1 chart (`clues` in `subjects.py`):
*facing* (an animal faces one way, so it does not match itself mirrored left to right),
*tips* (cells with one neighbour: ends of legs, tails and beaks), *thin* (the share of the
silhouette that is stem or leg rather than solid), and *solidity* and *roughness* of the outline.
On their own they tell animals from the rest about as well as one would hope (area under the curve
0.84 for *facing*), but adding them to the image model did not find more animals: the learner gave
them no weight, and the fair test holds only five animals, too few to show a difference. Animals
that come in mirrored pairs, two birds facing each other, also defeat *facing*.

The lesson is that the gap is labels, not features: 22 animals are too few for any measure to
outvote the plants around them. So the next step uses the measures the other way round, to find
candidates: 60 unlabelled charts nearest to the known animals (image model 0.7, clue measures 0.3;
`subjects.py animals`), almost all of them border bands, for the reviewer to mark *Animal* or
*No animal*.

## Words as features: an image-and-words model {#clip}

Looking for new features, we searched the research on pattern and shape classification
(sources below). The idea that worked best is an image-and-words model, CLIP: trained on pictures
with their captions, it can say how well a picture fits a phrase such as *"a cross-stitch
embroidery chart of a bird"*. We use the open re-trained version, OpenCLIP ViT-B/32 (`clip_features.py`).

The only human input is the list of phrases
([`prompts.csv`](https://github.com/HiDefTextiles/Sjonabok/blob/main/analysis/subjects/prompts.csv)):
words for what the reviewer looks for (a bird, a deer, a peacock, a flower, a vine, an
eight-pointed star, a rosette, letters of the alphabet and so on), chosen once. No chart's label is
shown to the model. This matches the plan: people decide *which* features matter, the computer
measures them on every chart.

Asked to name the group outright, CLIP is poor (55% on the fair test; it calls most plants
ornament). But its scores *relative to each other* are useful: they rank animals above the rest
with an area under the curve of 0.90, better than any other measure we have. So each chart gets
four scores (animals, plants, ornament, letters), each compared with its average over all charts,
and the distance between charts' scores became one more distance for the learner. A larger CLIP
(ViT-L/14) was no better, so the smaller, faster one is kept.

The learner kept the CLIP distances in every round since (see [Ways to browse](#browse)). On the
held-out fair test the right main group is found for 82% of charts (95% interval 68–92%) against
74% for the image model alone, and knots 80% against 63%.

Two animal pages (`subjects.py animals`, then `animal-answers`) showed the reviewer the unlabelled
charts nearest to the known animals, mostly border bands: 12 of the first 60 and 16 of the next 60
were animals, then 15 of a third 60 and 5 of a fourth, so there are now 70 and the search has
mostly run dry. Leaving each labelled chart out in turn, its five nearest charts now find animals
89% of the time (41% before the animal pages). One band family (B2) holds 40 of the 48 band animals.
The fair test holds only 5 animals, too few to confirm this.

Ideas we found and noted but have not used yet:

- **Symmetry groups of repeats** (Liu and Collins): the 7 frieze groups for bands and 17 wallpaper
  groups for all-over patterns. The gallery already measures the frieze group of each band; the
  wallpaper groups would matter if all-over patterns are added.
- **Skeleton shape** (Wilder, Feldman and Singh): the medial axis of a silhouette tells animals
  (a trunk with a few long limbs) from leaves (one axis with many short branches). Our *tips* and
  *thin* measures are a rough version; a proper skeleton is a candidate next feature.
- **Global shape descriptors for animals versus plants** (arXiv 1901.11398): simple measures such as
  convexity, elongation and moments separate the two classes surprisingly well in photographs.
- **Ornament datasets** (OrnAsia) and **CLIP tuned on art** (CLIP-Art): a model tuned on
  ornament could do better than general CLIP, but would need many labelled charts.

## Sub-motifs that recur {#submotifs}

Many charts are built from smaller figures that turn up again elsewhere: the same eight-pointed
star, the same pair of birds, the same deer, sometimes in several manuscripts. So the computer cuts
every chart into its pieces (filled cells that touch, at least 8 of them) and matches each piece
against all others, allowing it to be turned, mirrored and shifted by up to two cells; two pieces
match when they share at least 70% of their filled cells (`submotifs.py`). Matching pieces form one
sub-motif. No labels are used.

Of 1,785 pieces, 122 sub-motifs recur in two or more charts, and 106 of those in two or more
manuscripts. A chart can then be described by the sub-motifs it contains, and two charts that share
rare sub-motifs are close. For now this only reaches the 244 charts that share any piece, and
figures drawn joined to a branch or a border line are not cut out as pieces. Next steps are to
cut charts to their smallest repeat first, and to find figures that are joined to others. The
sub-motif by manuscript table is a first step toward asking how motifs travelled and changed
between manuscripts from the 17th to the 19th century.

## Ways to browse, found by the computer {#browse}

Subjects need a person. The ways of browsing below do not: the computer measures them from the
charts alone, the same way every time, so they cover all 600 charts, bands included. They are
filters in the gallery and also a way to put like with like, for example to choose a set of
related charts for [pattern synthesis](https://github.com/HiDefTextiles/pattern-synthesis).

| Filter | What it measures | Words |
|---|---|---|
| Look-alike family | The distances weighted as below; Ward clustering, motifs and bands separately; the number of families chosen by how stable they are | M1 to M4 for motifs, B1 to B3 for bands, with 24 close families in each part |
| Fit on 85 needles | A motif's width; a band's height across. With a band on both edges the motif corridor is 85 minus twice the band height | Motif up to 20, 21–40, 41–60, over 60 wide; band up to 7, 8–12, 13–17, over 17 rows |
| Outline | The figure with its holes filled: does it fill 82% or more of its box? | Fills its square, Stands free, Band |
| Stroke | The middle length of the runs of filled cells along rows and columns | Thin (under 1.5 cells), Double, Bold (2.5 or more) |
| Openness | Small enclosed openings per 100 filled cells. A tile or band is counted repeated, so openings across an edge count; a free-standing figure is counted once | Closed (under 1), Some openings, Lacy (5 or more) |

The sort order *Look-alike order* walks along the family tree, so each chart sits next to the
ones most like it, and each family starts with its name.

**People chose the features, the computer sets the groups.** The families use no labels. The
labels decided which measures count, and they come from the review: the reviewer saw that knots
and stars can show only when a motif is repeated, so the image model also looks at the chart
repeated (2 × 2, or a band twice along its length); and an outside review pointed out that
turning charts every way hides which way is up, which is what tells a plant (stem at the bottom)
or an animal (legs below) from an ornament, so the image model also looks at the chart only
upright and mirrored left to right, and three measures of uprightness were added (left-right and
top-bottom mirror kept apart, how top-heavy, how narrow the base).

For each weighting of the thirteen distances on a grid (including the [clue measures](#clues) and the [CLIP](#clip) image and word distances), the computer scored three things on the
labelled charts, leaving out the fair test: how often a chart's five nearest charts share its main
group, the same for the *knot* answers, and how well a cut of the motif tree into three follows
the main groups (the adjusted Rand index: 0 is chance, 1 is perfect). Several weightings tie at
the top (within 0.01, about the change one chart makes), so their mean is kept (`make weights.csv`
in `analysis/subjects`). With 54 knot answers and 70 animals the result is an even mix of six: the image model, the upright
image model, symmetry, form, the CLIP image model and the CLIP word scores, 0.17 each. The mix moves
from one round of labels to the next (after 65 animals it was the image model 0.4, CLIP word scores
0.4 and form 0.2), because many weightings score almost the same; the scores below barely move.

How good is it? On the 38 held-out fair-test charts, with the [CLIP word scores](#clip) and the
70 animals now labelled:

| Weighting | Right main group (95% interval) | Balanced over the four groups | Motifs cut in 3 vs main groups (ARI) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Learnt weights | 82% (68–92%) | 67% | 0.55 |
| Image model alone | 74% (58–87%) | 55% | 0.11 |
| All thirteen distances equally | 71% (55–84%) | 50% | 0.52 |
| Always guess ornament | 47% | 25% | 0 |

The learnt weights now beat the image model alone, though the intervals still overlap: 38 charts
are few. The balanced column shows where the work is: the fair test holds only 5 animals (2 found)
and 2 letter charts (1 found). More fair-test charts, chosen at random, would make these
numbers firmer.

The families themselves are kept only as fine as they are stable. The charts were resampled 50
times (`fpc::clusterboot` in R) and a family counts as stable when it is found again with a mean
Jaccard similarity of 0.7 or more. For the motifs that allows 4 families (0.73): ornament (M1),
small figures with animals and letters (M2) and two kinds of plant motif (M3, M4); bands give 3
(0.81). With the weights of the round before, one motif family was almost all animals; the number
and the cut move as the weights move. The number moves as the labels and weights change; the stable core (ornament, figures,
plants) has stayed.
The 24 close families in each part are finer and less stable: good for browsing, not a claim.
Ward's method assumes ordinary (Euclidean) distances, which rank-averaged distances are not; we
use it as a practical rule, checked by the resampling.

Words we tried and dropped after checking random examples by eye: *line* (by filled neighbours;
double strokes counted as lines), outline *round* and *diamond* (tulips and vases landed there)
and *detail* (it did not separate simple from intricate charts).

## Open and repeatable {#reproducible}

- **Code and settings are public.** All steps are in
  [`analysis/subjects/`](https://github.com/HiDefTextiles/Sjonabok/tree/main/analysis/subjects):
  `subjects.py` (steps 1, 2, 5, 6), `embed.py` (step 3) and `cluster.R` (step 4), run in order
  by a `Makefile`.
- **The same input gives the same output.** Clustering has no random element; the image model
  runs on the processor in PyTorch's deterministic mode; the model name and a fingerprint (SHA-256)
  of its weights are recorded with each run.
- **Only human work is stored.** Distances, piles and contact sheets are rebuilt from the charts
  in minutes, so they are not kept in git. `review.csv` and `subjects.csv` are kept, with names
  and dates, and every change to them is visible in the repository history.
- **Labels belong to charts, not piles.** Pile numbers change between runs; labels are stored by
  the chart's file name, so a new run cannot move or lose them.

## Try it on your own collection {#guide}

The method works for any set of small images: other pattern books, stamps, logos, fossils. What
you need: Python 3 with NumPy and Pillow, R with the tidyverse, and for step 3 PyTorch and timm
(`pip install torch timm`; the model, about 85 MB, downloads itself the first time).

```bash
git clone https://github.com/HiDefTextiles/Sjonabok
cd Sjonabok/analysis/subjects
make embed                # steps 1 and 3: units and the image model
make                      # steps 2 and 4 and the contact sheets
make review               # step 5: review on a phone or laptop, export review.csv
make labels REVIEWER="Your Name"
make suggest              # suggestions for the next round
make sample               # the fair test: random charts, labelled one at a time
```

Lessons from our pilot that carry over:

1. **Start small.** Run the whole loop on a few hundred items before scaling up. Our pilot is the
   233 motifs and rosettes.
2. **Over-split on purpose.** Many small piles are faster to label than a few large mixed ones.
3. **Label piles, fix exceptions.** Naming a pile of 12 birds is one decision, not twelve.
4. **Keep a fixed vocabulary.** Decide the subject words before reviewing, and add a word only on
   purpose, so labels stay consistent between people and rounds.
5. **Keep people's decisions as data.** Store who decided what and when, separately from anything
   a computer can rebuild.
6. **Look at the failures.** Piles that mix subjects tell you what the method cannot see; write
   that down, as we do below.
7. **Record the model.** Name the model and its version so the result can be checked later.
8. **Test people too.** Label a random sample a second time, one item at a time. Where a person
   disagrees with themselves, the categories are too fine; group them (as we did with
   [main groups](#groups)) or sharpen the definitions.

## Known limits {#limits}

- Both distances compare *form*. Two subjects with the same outline (a tulip and a stylised tree)
  can share a pile; the reviewer separates them.
- Very small or very dense charts lose detail at 16 × 16 cells and in the image model.
- Some charts hold more than one figure; for now they are compared as one picture.
- The knot measure also ranks other lacy, open patterns highly, so many of its top charts are not
  knots.
- Bands are compared by one repeat. For about 60 bands no repeat was found (some alternate two
  motifs, some have a long repeat), so they are compared whole, and some band families gather
  them for that reason rather than for how they look.
- The knot answers so far come from charts the computer chose as likely knots, so they say
  little about how the other measures do on knots.
- The subject words are ours. They describe what the motif looks like today, not what it meant to
  the people who drew it centuries ago.

## Sources {#sources}

- Oquab, M. et al. (2023). [DINOv2: Learning Robust Visual Features without Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07193). arXiv:2304.07193.
- R Core Team. [`hclust`: Hierarchical Clustering](https://search.r-project.org/R/refmans/stats/html/hclust.html), R documentation.
- McInnes, L., Healy, J. and Astels, S. (2017). [hdbscan: Hierarchical density based clustering](https://joss.theoj.org/papers/10.21105/joss.00205). *Journal of Open Source Software* 2(11). An alternative we considered.
- Radford, A. et al. (2021). [Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020) (CLIP). Its outright guesses on pattern charts are unreliable, but its relative scores for phrases are used as features ([Words as features](#clip)).
- Cherti, M. et al. (2023). [Reproducible scaling laws for contrastive language-image learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.07143) and [OpenCLIP](https://github.com/mlfoundations/open_clip): the open CLIP weights used (ViT-B/32, LAION-2B).
- Liu, Y., Collins, R. T. and Tsin, Y. (2004). [A computational model for periodic pattern perception based on frieze and wallpaper groups](https://www.ri.cmu.edu/pub_files/pub2/liu_yanxi_2000_2/liu_yanxi_2000_2.pdf). Symmetry groups of repeats.
- Wilder, J., Feldman, J. and Singh, M. (2011). [Superordinate shape classification using natural shape statistics](https://ruccs.sas.rutgers.edu/images/archive/personal-manish-singh/papers/Wilder_etal_2011.pdf). *Cognition* 119. Animals versus leaves by skeleton shape.
- [A study on general visual categorization of objects into animal and plant groups using global shape descriptors](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.11398) (2019). arXiv:1901.11398.
- [OrnAsia: a dataset of Asian ornaments for image classification and cultural identification](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12621315/). An ornament dataset.
- Conde, M. V. and Turgutlu, K. (2021). [CLIP-Art: Contrastive Pre-training for Fine-Grained Art Classification](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2021W/CVFAD/papers/Conde_CLIP-Art_Contrastive_Pre-Training_for_Fine-Grained_Art_Classification_CVPRW_2021_paper.pdf). CVPR workshops.
